$comment: Everyday stories, noun Screen, part 1 of 4 (screen, screenAction, screenPanel, panelLayout, panelSlot, regionMount). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.panelLayout.children: A shop owner wants a stock panel with a small summary on the left and a detailed table on the right. Children are layouts placed inside a layout, like drawers inside a cabinet. The panel is split into smaller areas, and each area is arranged on its own.
stories.panelLayout.fields: In a panel of delivery drivers, the manager wants to see name, vehicle and phone, in that order, and not all twelve boxes. Fields lists the boxes a layout shows and the order they come in. Whatever is not listed stays out of sight.
stories.panelLayout.metadata: The person who arranged a panel wants to leave a note for whoever comes next, such as 'ask Ana before changing this'. Metadata is a free notebook attached to the layout. NPDev carries it along untouched and does nothing with it.
stories.panelLayout.slots: A clinic's patient panel is generated, but the receptionist also wants a small hand-made drawing of the waiting room above it. Slots are reserved places where a piece written by the app's own developers is mounted, above the generated part, below it or in its place. That piece receives the panel's live data and can ask it to refresh.
stories.panelLayout.type: A warehouse manager wants stock as a plain table, while the shift supervisor wants a wall-board with big numbers and charts. Type chooses the shape of the panel: table or grid show the rows, console and dashboard show the declared widgets instead. Table is used if you say nothing.
stories.panelLayout.widgets: A supervisor's wall-board shows 'orders waiting' as a big number, a bar chart of the day and a list of the latest events. Widgets are those pieces, declared one by one, and the browser computes them from the panel's own data. They are used by the console and dashboard shapes.
stories.panelSlot.component: A bakery app's developers wrote a little oven-timer drawing of their own, in their own file. Component is the name that piece was registered under, so NPDev knows which one to put in the reserved place.
stories.panelSlot.label: Above the hand-made oven timer the page shows a small heading, 'Oven status', so people know what they are looking at. Label is that optional heading. Leave it out and the piece appears without a title.
stories.panelSlot.placement: The hand-made oven timer can sit above the table, below it, or take the table's place altogether. Placement chooses: above, below or replace. Replace is allowed once per panel, because only one thing can take the place of the generated part.
stories.regionMount.cellGrid: A cinema wants its seat plan drawn as a board of little squares that staff can paint, not as a list. When a region is shown as a cell grid, this keyword carries the settings of that board. It only matters when the render choice is cell grid.
stories.regionMount.component: A farm app has its own hand-made 'field map' piece. When a region is drawn by a component, this keyword names which registered piece takes over the drawing. It is required whenever the render choice is component.
stories.regionMount.render: A region of the page can be drawn by NPDev itself, by a hand-made piece the app's developers wrote, or as a board of paintable cells. Render chooses between generated, component and cell grid. Generated is what you get when you say nothing.
stories.screen.actions: On the page of a customer order, the clerk sees the buttons 'Approve' and 'Cancel order'. Actions are the buttons of a screen, and each one starts a flow, a recipe of steps. One click does the whole job, and nothing is left for the clerk to remember.
stories.screen.admin: Besides the page customers see, a shop needs a plain back-office page where staff list, search and edit the same orders. Admin switches on those generated back-office pages for the screen's concept, with their route, selection, detail view and more. It applies to list and workbench screens.
stories.screen.aggregate: An invoice is not one row: it has a header and several lines that belong together. On a document screen, aggregate names that whole bundle, so the printed page can read the header and the lines together. The name must match the bundle's main concept.
stories.screen.bands: A printed invoice has a top part with customer and date, then a table of items, then the totals. Bands are those horizontal stripes of a document, each read from the invoice's header or from one of its lists of lines. They need the aggregate to be named.
stories.screen.columns: A list of customers on a phone should show name, city and balance, and not forty boxes. Columns picks what a list, board or inbox shows, at most seven, because a screen is not a spreadsheet. The back office still has every box.
stories.screen.component: The farm's 'field map' is too special for any ready-made screen. On a custom screen, component names the hand-made piece, registered by the app's developers, and that piece is what the screen shows.
stories.screen.concept: A bookshop's 'Orders' screen has to know what an order is. Concept names the kind of record the screen shows or edits, such as Order. Its columns, filters and buttons are all about those records.
stories.screen.countdown: A concert ticket is held for ten minutes while the buyer pays, and the buyer wants to watch the clock. Countdown shows a live timer running down to a chosen moment, with a caption such as 'Time left to pay'.
stories.screen.empty: A new shop opens its 'Orders' list and sees a blank white page, which looks broken. Empty is what the screen shows when there are no rows: a friendly sentence and, if you want, a button such as 'Create the first order'.
stories.screen.fields: On a customer's detail page you want name, phone and address, in that order. Fields lists the boxes a detail, status or form screen shows. It is the counterpart of columns on lists.
stories.screen.filters: When someone picks a customer for an order, typing in the search box should look in the name and in the tax number. Filters names the boxes a person can search by in a picker.
stories.screen.grandTotal: A printed sales report ends with one last line: everything sold, added up. Grand total prints that row after the last group. It only works when at least one printed column is marked to be totalled.
stories.screen.groupBy: A task board has the columns To do, Doing and Done. On a board, group by names the choice box whose values become those columns. On a printed report it lists the fields the rows are grouped by, outermost first, such as region and then city. Only rows the viewer may read are counted.
stories.screen.kind: A restaurant needs a menu list, a booking form, a kitchen board and a dashboard of the day. Kind says which of these a screen is: list, detail, form, status, inbox, board, map, dashboard and others. That choice decides which of the other keywords apply.
stories.screen.live: A kitchen screen shows incoming orders, and refreshing by hand would make the soup late. Live makes the screen update itself the moment a row it shows changes, instead of asking again and again.
stories.screen.logo: A printed invoice looks serious with the company's logo in the corner. Logo is where a document screen says which logo to print on the page.
stories.screen.map: A courier app shows its delivery points as pins on a map. Map tells a map screen where the rows are placed and, on a form, which boxes a click on the map fills in.
stories.screen.marginMm: A printed invoice must leave room for the hole punch and the printer's edge. Margin sets the empty border around every printed page, in millimetres. It applies to document screens.
stories.screen.metadata: Whoever designed an invoice layout wants to note 'approved by finance, November'. Metadata is a free notebook on a document screen. NPDev carries it along unchanged and does nothing with it.
stories.screen.multiSelect: When assembling a delivery the dispatcher picks one driver, but for a team event the organiser picks several people. Multi-select lets a picker hand back several rows instead of exactly one. One is the default.
stories.screen.name: Every screen needs a name that people and other screens can use: 'Orders' appears in the address, and a menu can point to it. Name is that handle. It starts with a letter, and experiences and pickers refer to the screen by it.
stories.screen.orderBy: People open the invoice list and expect the newest on top. Order by names the box the rows are sorted by. A picker may give several boxes, and the first one sorts first.
stories.screen.pageSize: A company in Brazil prints on A4 while its branch in the United States prints on Letter. Page size sets the paper of a document screen: A4, which is the default, or Letter.
stories.screen.panel: Sometimes the back office needs a hand-built page that no generated screen offers, such as a special approvals board. On a custom screen, panel declares that page: its route, title, data, layout, buttons and visibility, all written on the screen itself. The screen supplies the panel's name.
stories.screen.params: A query called 'orders by city' needs to know which city. Params hands it the answer: for each parameter, a fixed value or an expression such as the current user's id. The screen then shows the right slice without anyone typing it.
stories.screen.pick: A 'My membership' page shows one record, but the address carries no id and several rows could match. Pick says which one to show: the first, the latest or the only one.
stories.screen.printColumns: A sales report on paper needs nine columns, far more than a phone screen would allow. Print columns lists them in order for a report document, each one a box of the concept. A column the viewer may not read is left out of the printout, never printed blank.
stories.screen.query: A 'Late deliveries' screen should not list every delivery, only the late ones, and that question has already been written once as a query. Query names it, and the screen shows the rows that query returns. Its parameters are filled in by params.
stories.screen.report: The finance team wants one definition that gives both a PDF to print and a spreadsheet to open. Report turns a document into a multi-record report over a concept. NPDev renders it as PDF and as CSV from that single definition.
stories.screen.returnMapping: A picker is opened from an order form so the clerk can choose a customer. Return mapping says what the picker hands back to the form, for example the customer's id as 'customerId' and the name as 'customerName'. Each value names a box of the picked row.
stories.screen.subtotals: A report grouped by region is easier to read when each region ends with its own sum. Subtotals prints a total row after each group. It needs a grouping and at least one printed column marked to be totalled.
stories.screen.title: 'Orders awaiting approval' tells the clerk more than 'Screen 7'. Title is the heading shown on the screen and in the navigation.
stories.screen.visibleWhen: The 'Payroll' screen should exist only for the people who run payroll. Visible when is a condition: while it is false the screen is hidden, and so is its entry in the menu.
stories.screen.where: A 'Pending orders' list should not show cancelled ones. Where is an extra filter on the rows. It can only narrow what the viewer may already see, never widen it. On a picker it is a simple list of conditions joined by 'and'.
stories.screen.widgets: A manager's dashboard shows today's sales as a big number, a chart of the week and a list of late orders. Widgets are those pieces, declared one by one on a dashboard screen.
stories.screenAction.confirm: Pressing 'Delete customer' by mistake would be a disaster. Confirm is the question shown right on the page, such as 'Delete this customer for good?', before the button actually does anything.
stories.screenAction.flow: A 'Ship order' button has to do real work: check stock, write the label, tell the customer. Flow names the recipe the button starts. If the person's role may not start that flow, the button is not shown to them.
stories.screenAction.input: When 'Ship order' starts its flow, the flow needs to know which order. Input hands it the answers: for each thing the flow asks for, an expression over the row the person is looking at. The button takes the details from the row, and nobody types them again.
stories.screenAction.label: 'Ship now' is clearer than 'Action 3'. Label is the caption written on the button.
stories.screenAction.moveTo: On a task board, dragging a card to the Done column should mark the task finished. Move to says which column, a value or an expression, a move sends the row to. The flow receives that column as its input.
stories.screenAction.style: 'Delete' should not look like 'Save'. Style gives the button its look: primary, secondary or danger in red. Move is a special style for dragging a card from one column of a board to another.
stories.screenAction.then: After the clerk presses 'Create invoice', the next useful place is the invoice itself. Then names the screen to open after the action succeeds. Without it, the person stays where they are and the page refreshes.
stories.screenAction.visibleWhen: A 'Cancel order' button makes no sense for an order that has already shipped. Visible when is a condition over the current row: the button appears only while it is true.
stories.screenPanel.actions: A back-office panel of pending refunds needs 'Approve' and 'Reject' buttons. Actions are the buttons of the panel, each one starting a flow, like the buttons of a normal screen.
stories.screenPanel.dataSources: The panel of pending refunds must know where its rows come from, for example the refunds and the customers they belong to. Data sources are those row suppliers. The layout then decides how they are drawn.
stories.screenPanel.enabledWhen: A 'Close month' panel should be touched only once every invoice has been posted. Enabled when is a condition: the panel can be used only while it is true, and is greyed out otherwise.
stories.screenPanel.explainability: A year from now, someone asks why the 'Refund review' panel exists. Explainability is a free note for AI helpers and auditors saying why the panel is there and what it shows. NPDev stores it and does not act on it.
stories.screenPanel.fieldBindings: In the refunds panel, the 'amount' box should be shown with its currency and 'reason' should come with a small hint. Field bindings tie boxes of the data sources to the panel, with their rules and hints.
stories.screenPanel.guidePage: The back office has a start page with tiles, a guide page, for the finance team. Guide page names the one that hosts this panel, so the panel shows up where the finance team already looks.
stories.screenPanel.layout: The same refund data can be a plain table or a wall-board with tiles. Layout says how the panel's data sources are laid out on the page.
stories.screenPanel.metadata: Whoever built a panel wants to keep a note beside it, such as 'requested by finance'. Metadata is a free notebook on the panel. NPDev carries it along unchanged and does nothing with it.
stories.screenPanel.route: Each page needs an address people can bookmark, such as '/refunds'. Route is the last piece of that address, the one this panel is served at.
stories.screenPanel.title: 'Refunds waiting for approval' is better than 'Panel 4'. Title is the heading of the panel.
stories.screenPanel.uid: A panel was called 'Refunds' and someone renames it to 'Returns'. Without a sticker on it, NPDev could think the old one was deleted and a new one appeared. Uid is a stable identity number, made once and never reused, so a rename is recognised as the same panel. It is optional.
stories.screenPanel.visibility: The 'Salaries' panel should be seen only by HR. Visibility is a condition on the panel: it is shown only while the condition is true.
